title: The crucifix in Naples
hook: tradition says Christ asked what reward he wanted and Thomas answered only you, Lord

segments.voice: Yesterday, to contemplate and hand on: Thomas's lamp, giving light and not only shining. Your line was light others. Who got the one thing you'd learned? Today closes the week. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-three.

"What do you want?" It's the question a cartoon genie asks, and the question a good friend asks when you finally go quiet at dinner. It sounds easy. It almost never is. The answer comes out as a list: a raise, a cure, a little more time, for a certain person to call back. There's a story about Thomas Aquinas in which someone asks him exactly that, and the one asking is Christ. His answer is very short. Today: the crucifix in Naples.
screen: `WHAT DO YOU WANT?` → `THE ANSWER COMES OUT AS A LIST.` → `CHRIST ASKS THOMAS.`

segments.voice: Here's the story as tradition tells it. It comes from the people who gathered memories of Thomas after his death, and it's set in Naples, in the Dominican house there. Thomas is praying before a crucifix in the chapel. A brother who happens to be nearby hears a voice from the cross. It says, in effect: Thomas, you have written well of me. What reward will you have for your work? And Thomas answers: non nisi te, Domine. Nothing but you, Lord. Be honest about what kind of story this is. It's a holy memory, handed down, not something you can check like a receipt. Catholics are free to weigh it as they like. But look at what the story chooses to say. This is the man of the long Summa, with its objections and replies, its five ways and its careful distinctions. And when the moment comes, he doesn't ask for his books to last, or for his arguments to win, or even for understanding. He asks for a person. That fits what Thomas wrote. In the Summa he says our final happiness is seeing God, and that charity is friendship with God. Friends don't really want the gifts. They want the friend. There's an old line in the Psalms, in the Douay-Rheims, that sounds the same note: "For what have I in heaven? and besides thee what do I desire upon earth?" Look back at this week. God who fittingly shares our nature. Sacraments as his tools. Bread whose substance changes. Hymns for Corpus Christi, a God here in hiding, a lamp that lights others. All of it, in this story, comes down to one answer.
screen: `A VOICE FROM THE CROSS.` · `NON NISI TE, DOMINE.` · `A PERSON, NOT A PRIZE.` · `THE WEEK IN ONE ANSWER.` · then, large: `BESIDES THEE WHAT DO I DESIRE?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: answer the question. Settle, and breathe. Let the question come to you plainly: what do you want? Let the list come too, because it will. The job, the health, the person. Don't push any of it away. Just let it be said. Then ask, underneath the list: what do you want most? It's all right if the answer surprises you, or doesn't come. If you pray, you can bring Thomas's short answer to God and see whether they fit. The bell holds the time.
The crucifix in Naples. The story, told by tradition, of Christ asking Thomas what reward he wanted, and Thomas answering, nothing but you, Lord. Today's word.
Your line: only you, Lord. Today, when you catch yourself wanting something hard, ask what it's standing in for. That's the week. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-three.

howItsDone: Some Catholics retell this story on Thomas's feast day, and Thomas's answer, non nisi te, Domine, is sometimes painted or carved near images of him.

original.note: Latin: nothing but you, Lord. Thomas's answer in the story.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pious legend about a famous saint.
what it means: the man of the Summa, offered any reward, asks only for Christ himself.
what a scholar hears: told by the early witnesses gathered after his death; accounts differ on details, and it echoes his own teaching that charity is friendship with God.

notes: The crucifix story is paraphrased from tradition (William of Tocco's Life; testimony at the canonization inquiry). Accounts vary in wording and some place it elsewhere (e.g. Orvieto or Paris); the script follows the index in setting it in Naples and frames it as 'tradition tells it'. Keeper to confirm.
Latin 'Bene scripsisti de me, Thoma... Non nisi te, Domine' as commonly given; confirm the reply's wording; the script avoids counting the words of the reply.
